planting.note: Pruning group three; flowers entirely on new growth, so cut the whole vine back to about a foot from the ground each late winter.

directions: This viticella selection bears small, nodding, lightly spicy-scented flowers in a dusky reddish-purple that fades to a paler purple toward the base of each sepal, produced from midsummer into early autumn on the current season's growth. The flowers are modest in size, around an inch and a half across, but appear in such profusion that the vine can be trained up a trellis or sunny fence for a long season of color. Like other viticella types, it resists clematis wilt and tolerates hard annual pruning, making it an easy, low-maintenance choice for weaving through shrubs or a sunny support.

common_name: Kathryn Chapman Clematis (Pale Cream Nodding Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Pruning group three; flowers entirely on new growth, so cut the whole vine back to about a foot from the ground each late winter.

directions: This viticella-group cultivar produces dainty, nodding, bell-shaped flowers that open pale cream and fade to white, with a faint streak of pink on the outer surface of each of the four to six blunt-tipped tepals. Green anthers tipped in dark burgundy provide gentle contrast against the pale petals, and the flowers hang attractively on long stems from midsummer into early fall. Free-flowering and resistant to clematis wilt, it tolerates the same hard annual pruning as other viticella types and is well suited to scrambling through a shrub or along a sunny fence.

planting.note: Pruning group three; tolerates partial shade better than many clematis and flowers entirely on new growth, so cut back hard each late winter.

directions: Named for a Cornish village and former tin mine, this vigorous, shade-tolerant viticella cultivar bears a profusion of large, nodding, bell-shaped flowers from midsummer into early fall. Each violet-blue bloom carries a broad white central stripe veined and flushed with violet-blue, with green stamens adding further contrast, and flowers can reach five inches across. It holds the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, reflecting its reliable performance in British gardens, and like other viticella types it tolerates hard annual pruning and resists clematis wilt.

common_name: GALORE Clematis (Dark Purple Fading Viticella-Type Clematis)

planting.note: A pruning group two type that flowers on old wood with a second later flush on new growth; give only a light tidy in late winter rather than hard cutback.

directions: Marketed under the trade name GALORE, this vigorous, free-flowering twining vine bears dark purple flowers with yellow anthers from June into September; the color gradually softens and fades toward the base of the sepals, giving each bloom a two-toned effect as it ages. Unlike true viticella selections that bloom only on new wood, this hybrid flowers on old wood first with a second flush later in the season, so pruning should be light rather than a hard cutback. Site it with its roots shaded and its climbing growth in full sun to part shade, and let it scramble through a shrub, rose, or small tree for support.

common_name: Brocade Clematis (Brick-Red Fading Pink Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Pruning group three; flowers entirely on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard each late winter.

directions: This viticella selection produces nodding, textured, veined flowers in a brick-red tone that fades toward deep pink as the blooms age, appearing from July through September on wiry stems that can climb to over ten feet. The four sepals give each flower a somewhat ruffled, rounded look distinct from the flatter form of many other viticella cultivars. It shares the group's typical ease of care, tolerating hard annual pruning and resisting clematis wilt, and performs well scrambling through an early-flowering shrub or along a sunny trellis.

common_name: Buckland Beauty Clematis (Rosy Pink Texas-Group Clematis)

planting.note: Set out in spring with the crown planted a couple of inches deep and roots shaded; being largely herbaceous, it is cut back hard to the base each year.

directions: A hybrid of the Texas native Clematis texensis with the related species C. pitcheri, this vine bears small, bell-shaped flowers in a rosy purplish-pink with a contrasting cream edge, produced freely from June through the summer on wiry, twining stems. Like its texensis parent, it is more heat- and drought-tolerant than many large-flowered clematis once established, and because it blooms on new growth it should be cut back hard to the base each late winter to renew vigor. Train it on a narrow support such as an obelisk or wire trellis in full sun, keeping the root zone cool and shaded.

planting.note: Pruning group three; flowers entirely on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard each late winter.

directions: A healthy, exceptionally free-flowering viticella selection, this cultivar produces masses of nodding, deep carmine-red flowers edged and veined in a darker red, with contrasting dark red-purple anthers, from July through September. Individual blooms are small, around two inches across, but the sheer quantity produced makes the vine an effective way to add color to a fence, obelisk, or shrub through the second half of the growing season. It shares the viticella group's wilt resistance and tolerance for hard annual pruning, making it a low-fuss choice for covering vertical space quickly each year.

common_name: Richard's Picotee Clematis (Creamy White Purple-Edged Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Pruning group three; flowers entirely on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard each late winter.

directions: This very floriferous viticella selection bears small, nodding, bell-shaped flowers that are creamy white with distinct purple-pink picotee edges along each of the typically four, though sometimes five or six, sepals. Blooms appear in great numbers from midsummer into early autumn on dark green, pinnate foliage, and the vine readily sends up many new shoots each season. As with other viticella types, it resists clematis wilt and responds well to a hard annual cutback, making it an easy choice for weaving through a sunny shrub or along a fence.

common_name: Bolam Belle Clematis (Dark Violet Silvery-Hued Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Pruning group three; flowers entirely on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard each late winter. Self-sown seedlings nearby may not come true to type.

directions: A very floriferous viticella cultivar, this selection bears small, nodding or drooping, bell-shaped flowers in a dark violet overlaid with a distinctive silvery-grey hue, each only about two inches across. It flowers abundantly from midsummer into early fall and seeds itself readily in the garden, though volunteer seedlings are variable and will not necessarily match the parent plant. Like other viticella types it tolerates hard annual pruning and resists clematis wilt, making it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for a trellis, obelisk, or sunny shrub to scramble through.
